content: 1. A study found a positive correlation between the consumption of sweet foods during infancy (3 to 12 months) and an increased weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) at 3 years of age. However, no such association was observed with other types of snack foods. 2. Among children aged 2 to less than 5 years, seven studies investigated the relationship between high versus low consumption of unhealthy foods and outcomes such as body mass index (BMI), overweight/obesity, and percentage body fat. Two studies reported that the consumption of sugar added to milk and fruit was associated with higher BMI in both boys and girls aged 2 to less than 6 years, but this association was only observed in boys aged 6 to less than 10 years. 3. Three studies presented varying results depending on the quantity of unhealthy food consumed, the outcome measured, or the age at follow-up. One study found that consuming foods high in fat was associated with a higher BMI z-score (BMIZ) but not with overweight or obesity. Another study reported no association between the frequency of energy-dense food consumption and BMIZ, but a positive association was found between the percentage of energy intake from ultra-processed foods at 4 years and BMIZ at 7 years. 4. One study found no effects of added sugar consumption at 2 years of age on changes in BMIZ at 5 and 6 years of age. Similarly, sugar consumption at 1 year of age was not associated with changes in BMIZ at 7 years. However, changes in sugar intake between 1 and 7 years of age were positively associated with changes in BMIZ. 5. The remaining studies reported no association between unhealthy food consumption and BMI, overweight, or obesity. Five studies examined the relationship between unhealthy food consumption in children aged 5 to 10 years and weight-related outcomes, but no consistent associations were found. 6. Across all age groups, four studies examined the relationship between unhealthy food consumption and body fat. Three studies measured percentage body fat, and one assessed fat mass index. None of the studies found an association between unhealthy food consumption and body fat. 7. A dietary modeling study excluded unhealthy foods and beverages from optimal diets but added specific unhealthy items (e.g., sweet biscuits/cookies and fried crisps/chips) at varying frequencies (1, 3, and 7 servings per week) while maintaining constant energy intake. Among infants aged 6 to 8 months, the inclusion of one serving of unhealthy foods per week had minimal impacts. However, consuming these foods seven times per week resulted in nutrient gaps for calcium, potassium, zinc, and thiamine, and worsened the gap in iron intake. 8. For children aged 12 to 23 months, the inclusion of up to seven servings of unhealthy foods per week had few impacts on nutrient intakes. However, the overall evidence on the association between unhealthy foods and beverages and health outcomes was mixed. 9. Several studies suggested that the consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) and unhealthy foods might increase BMI, BMIZ, percentage body fat, dental caries, and the odds of overweight or obesity. However, only one of five studies found that beverages with non-sugar sweeteners had an adverse outcome (higher BMI). 10. Consumption of sweet foods during infancy may be positively associated with WHZ later in life. Adverse anthropometric outcomes were observed among children aged 2 to less than 5 years and 5 to 10 years. However, the consumption of 100% fruit juice was not associated with any evaluated outcomes. 11. Among breastfed infants aged 6 to 11 months, dietary modeling showed that the inclusion of unhealthy foods increased nutrient gaps for iron and zinc, as well as several other nutrients. This was also true for iron among breastfed infants aged 9 to 11 months. For non-breastfed children aged 12 to 23 months, there were few impacts on nutrient intakes. 12. The certainty of the evidence was determined to be low or very low, primarily due to risks of bias across studies, including confounding and selection bias resulting from non-randomized designs. 13. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the evidence showed no benefits and uncertain harms for the consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages with non-sugar sweeteners during the complementary feeding period. For SSBs, there was no evidence of benefits and moderate evidence of harms. No benefits or harms were associated with the consumption of 100% fruit juice. 14. Modeling studies indicated that the introduction of unhealthy foods and SSBs among infants and young children increased nutrient gaps. The GDG recommended less consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages with non-sugar sweeteners and no consumption of SSBs. They also recommended limiting the consumption of 100% fruit juice. 15. Caregivers in several countries reported feeding unhealthy foods to children due to their high palatability, convenience, and affordability. Packaging that implies safety also increased the acceptability of snack foods in some settings. Efforts are needed to support caregivers in implementing these recommendations. 16. Unhealthy foods, often highly processed, contain high amounts of free sugars, salt, trans fats, and saturated fats. SSBs are high in free sugars and energy but provide little nutritional value. Both displace healthy foods, making it difficult to meet nutrient needs. Evidence shows they are associated with both undernutrition and overweight. Early consumption of non-sugar sweeteners may create a preference for sugary foods later in life. 17. Although 100% fruit juice contains free sugars, it provides some nutrients and does not appear to affect adiposity in children. The recommendation to avoid SSBs and limit 100% fruit juice aligns with WHO guidelines on sugar intake and policies to promote healthy diets. 18. Nutrient supplements and fortified food products may help fill nutrient gaps in settings where diverse, nutrient-rich complementary foods are not regularly available or affordable. Multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs), fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods, fortified milk, and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were reviewed as part of this guideline. 19. MNPs are single-dose sachets containing multiple vitamins and minerals, designed to be mixed with semi-solid foods for children aged 6 months and older. They are recommended in populations where anemia is a public health problem, based on moderate-certainty evidence. 20. Fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods and fortified milk are commercially available globally, while SQ-LNS and MNPs are distributed through nutrition programs. These products are intended to complement a child’s diet and should not replace a diverse diet of healthy, minimally processed foods. 21. A systematic review estimated that 56% of children aged 6 to 59 months globally are deficient in at least one of three micronutrients (iron, zinc, and vitamin A). However, this estimate is uncertain due to a lack of population-based data. 22. The WHO guidelines recommend the use of fortified complementary foods or vitamin-mineral supplements as needed to address nutrient deficiencies during the complementary feeding period.
